newsitem.title: UK: YEAREND - UK stocks seen consolidating in 1997.
newsitem.headline: YEAREND - UK stocks seen consolidating in 1997.

text.p: Britain's stock market looks set to consolidate next year despite nervousness over possible further setbacks on Wall Street and concern about interest rates rising.
But most analysts say they are not unduly concerned about a likely Labour Party victory in a general election.
The average forecast of analysts polled by Reuters said the benchmark FTSE 100 index would end 1997 at 4,250, up by around five percent from its current level.

The index closed 8.2 points higher at 3,990.7 on Thursday afternoon after dropping sharply on Wednesday in response to losses on Wall Street. Last Friday, it suffered its biggest one-day loss in four years as world markets tumbled following remarks about "irrational overexuberance" in stocks by U.S. Federal Reserve Chairman Alan Greenspan.

Brokerage houses mostly expected British economic growth to sustain shares in the coming year, although some analysts doubted that the gains of 1996 could be matched as inflation could take off and lead to tighter monetary policy.

Richard Jeffrey, head of research at Charterhouse Tilney, said the market could move higher in the first half. "The political environment could cause some disruption, but I don't expect it to be unduly adverse," he said.

"In the second half of the year I think growing problems with inflation and the upward pressure that puts on interest rates will begin to take its toll on the equity markets and gains made in the first half will probably be lost," he added.

But some strategists expected weakness in the first half of the year, partly due to profit-taking. "But that just means there's more to go for in the second half," HSBC James Capel UK equity strategist Robert Buckland said.
"It's not exactly a bullish forecast. We've just got the market ticking along with earnings and dividends. We've got no help from interest rates," he said.
CORPORATE PROSPECTS ALLAY ELECTION JITTERS
JP Morgan European equity market strategist Gary Dugan said the election injected a note of caution but firms could do well.

"It's difficult to talk about positive factors in an election year, but the UK economy is showing very robust growth. We've got about 3.7 percent GDP growth next year, which we think will translate into good corporate profits growth," he said.

"The market at the moment is only looking for about nine percent earnings growth. We think there could be a surprise on the upside and this is what could drive some improvement in the market," he added.

"The problem is that domestic institutions have not been investing and overseas institutions are wary ahead of an election, so it's difficult to see the market making a huge amount of progress ahead of a likely election in May."
Panmure Gordon equity strategist Ian Williams said the election would not make a big difference and interest rates would go up anyway, but perhaps faster under a Labour government.

SocGen strategist Andy Hartwill said a victory by Labour, leading in opinion polls by a wide margin, would probably produce a modest knee-jerk downwards reaction. "Then there will be a correction, but all bets are off until we've seen the black and white of their first budget."

Ian Scott of Lehman Brothers thought industrial stocks, sensitive to economic growth, would perform well, but he said much depended on the bond market and the overall outlook was clouded by the election. "The pre-election period may not throw a lot of light on the precise details of policies," he said.
INDUSTRIALS AND FINANCIALS MAY BEAT CONSUMERS
HSBC's Buckland said the financial sector of the market could perform well, but others feared the impact of inflation.
"They may see a little bit of weakness in the first quarter of the year as people take profits, but they'll still be showing quite decent gains over the year," Buckland said.
BZW global strategist Michael Hughes said consumer stocks might do less well than industrials in 1997.
"It is the industrial stocks that have been left behind (this year) and they have underperformed quite strongly in the last month as sterling has appreciated," he said.
Hughes said the dollar-sensitive stocks had been at a disadvantage recently but not all exporters had suffered. "We have continued to gain market share against some European competitors," he said.
All analysts expected a good year in manufacturing.
JP Morgan's Dugan summed up the mood, saying: "There may be a few interest rate increases, but we may be able to overcome these if growth is good and it starts to flow through to corporate profits."
Analysts agreed that Wall Street was unlikely to soar upwards as much as in 1996, advancing more in line with U.S. corporate profits growth estimated at six-seven percent.
But Panmure Gordon's Williams said Wall Street had the potential to surge beyond recent records, saying it was difficult to see what could stop it in the short term.

"But as far as the UK is concerned, we're at a different point in the economic cycle. The relative performance of the markets over the past two or three years has been quite diverse, so you'd think if shouldn't have that much effect," he said.
"Although in reality that may not be the case."
